subject: Wishlist : a bindable reference manual, a searchable electronic reference manual

messages.author: bcfb6bc9f75aae0f
messages.subject: Wishlist : a bindable reference manual, a searchable electronic reference manual
parts:
Dear Stan authors,

The current reference manual is quite nice. But for some knuckledraggers who sometimes use their docs on paper (I happen to be one of them),  it has a quirk :

In the existing PDFs, parts and chapter start immediately after the end of the previous chapter.

Ouch ! This a) slows down searching references by page and b) is ugly as hell...

In common European/American printing usage, odd pages are placed on the right-hand page ("good" page) of a bound document (book). This can be obtained in \LaTeX by using the "twosides" option of the document class (numerous document class support this option, including all classes derived from the "standard classes" of current \LaTeX distributions). This inserts blank pages before the start of a chapter (or a part) when the previous page was an odd page, and fixes the page numbering sequence accordingly.

Since, as far as I know, the source of the reference manual is not accessible, could we have a "boundable" version of the reference manual for this (admittedly retarded) purpose ?

Similarly, for the more enlightened part of the Stan users set, an electronic version of the reference manual could be useful (especially, one could search through the manual with almost any ebook reader, without being constrained by the embedded physical format imposed by the PDF...).

An epub version comes to mind. This also can be produced from a \LaTeX source (with some hooplas for the math code, which is somewhat sparse in the Stan reference manual) : see for example what pandoc or calibre can accomplish (with a bit of an effort...). Such a document can be read on a lot of supports (computer, tablet, even a phone...), i. e. independently of the computer where Stan is installed...

A much more ambitious alternative would be a cross-referenced hypertext (e. g. an HTML page set locally installed on the user's computer). But that's a lot more effort, and probably not worth it until Stan is more stable, with predictable life duration of a given version more than a couple of months.

HTH,

--
Emmanuel Charpentier

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Wishlist : a bindable reference manual, a searchable electronic reference manual
parts:
Every part of Stan is open source and the manual comes with
a very liberal CC-BY license. The manual is on GitHub here:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/develop/src/docs/stan-reference

You could even sell bound copies and Kindle versions on Amazon if you
wanted under the CC-BY as long as the Stan Dev team retains copyright
and is listed as the author.

If you know how to add the blank pages you want (probably just
cleardoublepage and twosided formats somewhere), please
let me know what I need to fix or even better, submit a pull request.
I don't really have time to fiddle with formatting right now.

One issue you're going to have is that the version we distribute
uses the proprietary Lucida fonts. There's branching logic
in the manual's style to allow it to be generated using
built-in LaTeX fonts, but the formatting of line lengths and
so forth will be off (and the built-in Computer Modern and
Courier are terrible fonts due to too light vertical bars
and mismatched x-heights; Times Roman is too narrow for
good readability and doesn't match courier in color [typesetting
term]).

If you'd like to figure out how to produce an ePub version
and could send us a pull request, we could include the
script in our distributions.

We're unlikely to ever support versions for more than a couple
months due to lack of resources---we roll rather like R that
way. But that's not lack of stability---we've maintained
backward compatibility in the major versions (1.x.y and 2.x.y)
throughout and the language all the way back to the beginning.
We just keep adding new features.

We do want to produce an online version, perhaps using the same
system as Hadley Wickham's Advanced R. It's just too much
trouble given all the LaTeX and the other demands on our time.
We're experimenting with that in the econometrics book we're
writing with James Savage.

Personally, I strongly prefer LaTeX for online reading over Kindle
formats because they're easier to zoom. In fact, I created that
format to work well on my iPad in GoodReader and to be easily printable
two-up.

- Bob
